title: Truthful Bidding Is Dominant in the Online Auction
body_html:
Truthful Bidding Is Dominant in the Online Auction

Theorem (dsic). In the online single-item auction (Online Single-Item (Posted-Price) Auction) — for any history-dependent pricing rule — truthful bidding $b_i = v_i$ is a weakly dominant strategy for every bidder.

Formally, for every pricing rule $A$, every arrival/bid profile $f$ indexed by the $n$ bidders, every true-valuation profile $v$, and every bidder $i$, the payoff to $i$ can only increase by switching $i$'s bid to the truthful value $v_i$ (keeping everyone else's bid fixed):

$$ A.\mathrm{utility}(f,\, v,\, i) \;\le\; A.\mathrm{utility}\bigl(f[i \mapsto ((f\,i).\text{id},\, v_i)],\; v,\; i\bigr). $$
proof_html:
The argument is a locality observation followed by a single-variable optimisation.

  1. The posted price bidder $i$ faces is independent of $b_i$. The state of the auction just before bidder $i$ arrives is determined by the first $i$ bids — none of which is $b_i$. Replacing $b_i$ with any other bid therefore leaves the price posted to $i$ unchanged. A posted-price rule cannot let a bidder move their own price.

  2. Single-bidder optimisation at a fixed price. With the posted price $p$ and the tie-breaking condition fixed, bidder $i$'s payoff is $v_i - p$ when the acceptance test ($p < b_i$, or $p = b_i$ with the tie-break in $i$'s favour) succeeds, and $0$ otherwise. The surplus $v_i - p$ is nonneg precisely when $p \le v_i$, so bidding $b_i = v_i$ accepts exactly when accepting is profitable. Any other bid either gives up a profitable trade or accepts a money-losing one.

Combining the two steps: bidder $i$ cannot influence the price they face, and at that price truthful bidding maximises their payoff.

Remarks

Why it matters

The truthfulness here is format-independent: it holds for every history-dependent posted-price rule, not just a particular one. This is the defining advantage of posted-price mechanisms over the sealed-bid second-price auction (Vickrey Truth-Telling Is Dominant) — truthfulness comes for free from the order of moves (price first, bid second) rather than from a carefully engineered payment rule. It is what licenses treating reported bids as true valuations in the downstream welfare analyses (No Deterministic Constant Competitive Ratio, Sample-Then-Threshold Rule Is 1/4-Competitive).

Lean formalization

The two steps of the proof are isolated as separate lemmas in EconCSLib. The locality step is stateBeforeStep_update_self: the state reached before processing bidder $i$ depends only on the first $i$ bids, so replacing $i$'s own bid leaves this state — and hence the posted price — invariant. The single-bidder optimisation step is local_dsic, stated parametrically in an abstract tie-breaking predicate tie_ok; this isolates the optimisation from the specifics of how the threshold's identity component resolves ties. The top-level theorem dsic rewrites via stateBeforeStep_update_self and then applies local_dsic with the tie-break condition derived from the threshold's identity component.

References

  • [Roughgarden 2016, Lecture 2, Problem 2.1(a)] Tim Roughgarden, Twenty Lectures on Algorithmic Game Theory, Cambridge University Press. Dominant-strategy truthfulness of online posted-price auctions.
